Model Output:
### Part 1: How a Human Approaches This vs. Telltale LLM Failings When a human writer tackles a prompt like *"Cozy-Horror: eating the spore mutants trying to kill us,"* they usually write from a place of specific, lived experience combined with a slightly perverse sense of humor. A human who loves cooking knows the *actual* unglamorous mechanics of a kitchen: how fat renders, how a dull knife slips on silver-skin, how your knuckles ache when it’s cold, and how grief or terror makes your stomach feel like a knotted rag. A human also understands that "cozy" isn’t a curated Pinterest board of copper pots and beeswax candles; true coziness in a crisis is **relief**. It’s taking off wet boots, the smell of bleach and woodsmoke, and eating something hot out of a chipped mug while your hands stop shaking. **Telltale LLM Approaches & Why They Hurt This Piece:** 1. **The "Sensory Wallpaper" Trap (Over-writing):** * *LLM Habit:* LLMs love to string together compound adjectives and relentless sensory descriptions to prove they are setting a scene: *"The bioluminescent tendrils pulsed with an eerie, otherworldly glow against the warm, amber-lit flagstones of the rustic cottage."* * *Why it fails here:* When everything is described at a 10/10 intensity, nothing stands out. Both the horror and the food become weightless. If the prose is too "impressive" and ornate, you don't actually feel hungry when they cook, and you don't feel grossed out when they butcher the monster. 2. **Writing Safely / Sanitizing the Premise:** * *LLM Habit:* LLMs are deeply conflict-averse and try to sand off moral edges so the characters remain 100% pure and likable. * *Why it fails here:* The prompt is inherently transgressive! Even if we avoid straight-up cannibalism, eating a "spore mutant" should feel deeply taboo, gross, and psychologically weird at first. If the monster is just a "walking Wagyu-mushroom," there is no psychological hurdle to overcome. 3. **The "Restaurant Review" Food Description:** * *LLM Habit:* When asked to write delicious food, LLMs default to luxury buzzwords: *umami, transcendent, A5 Wagyu, King Crab, black truffle, caramelized perfection, symphony of flavors.* * *Why it fails here:* To a starving person, food doesn't taste like a Michelin-star menu; it tastes like *salt, grease, heat, and survival*. Comparing a mutant immediately to Wagyu beef and lobster feels artificial and breaks the gritty reality of an apocalypse. 4. **Wrapping Every Chapter in a Neat Bow:** * *LLM Habit:* LLMs love ending chapters on summarizing thesis statements: *"As they held hands by the fire, they knew that no matter what horrors waited outside, they had each other—and a full pantry."* * *Why it fails here:* It kills tension and makes the story feel like a series of Hallmark cards rather than a continuous, strange narrative. --- ### Part 2: Deep-Dive Critique of the Current Plan Looking closely at the **Intention** and **Chapter Plan** we just generated, it is full of classic AI structural tropes and safety nets: 1. **The "Conveniently Innocent" Monster Biology:** * *The Critique:* In the plan, I explicitly avoided human-mutants and decided the creatures are "pure fungal chimeras" made of forest biomass (deer, boars, bark) that magically have the cellular density of prime beef and crab. Furthermore, I gave Simon a convenient "mycologist" background so he can scientifically explain *why* heat and vinegar make it 100% safe. * *Why it's an LLM pitfall:* This completely neuters the horror! If the creature is basically just an aggressive wild boar made of gourmet mushrooms, and Simon knows scientifically how to make it safe, where is the desperation? Where is the nasty, taboo thrill of the prompt? 2. **The "Cottagecore Catalog" Characters:** * *The Critique:* Bea (warm, stubborn chef with cast-iron skillets) and Simon (quiet, gentle park ranger/botanist) living in a stone cottage with copper pots, patchwork quilts, and dandelion wine. * *Why it's an LLM pitfall:* They have zero friction. They read like two cosy tropes stapled together. Long-term couples who are starving to death in a locked house get irritable! They have weird habits, unspoken fears, and dark humor. Right now, they are too wholesome. 3. **The "Instant Gratification" Time Jump (Chapter 4 to 5):** * *The Critique:* In Chapter 4 they take one bite and have a "transcendent culinary experience." By Chapter 5, it’s three months later, they are "plump and rosy-cheeked," making "Clicker-tendril confit" and "Spore-belly bacon," and writing a leather-bound cookbook. * *Why it's an LLM pitfall:* This skips the most interesting part of the story—the awkward, weird transition from "we are eating a nightmare out of sheer desperation" to "wait, why am I craving this?" Also, "Spore-belly bacon" and "Clicker-tendril confit" sound like cute video game items (like *Dungeon Meshi* or *Fallout*), which undercuts the grounded horror. 4. **The Stock "Outsider Foil" & "Boss Fight" Climax (Chapters 6–8):** * *The Critique:* Devon falls into a trap, gets wrapped in a quilt, cries over stew, sees a severed monster head in the mudroom, panics, and then helps them kill an "Apex Crowned Goliath" with a "heart-truffle," ending with everyone clinking glasses of dandelion wine. * *Why it's an LLM pitfall:* This is a very standard, algorithmic plot escalator. The "Apex Boss Monster" in Chapter 7 turns a creepy, intimate survival story into an action movie, and the ending wraps up way too neatly, erasing Devon’s trauma with one bite of truffle risotto. --- ### Part 3: Brainstorming Ideas to Make It More Human To elevate this from a predictable AI story to something that feels authored by a sharp, weird, empathetic human writer, here are ways we can roughen the edges and deepen the psychology: #### 1. Make the Monsters Uncomfortably Close to the Bone * We don't need them to be neighbors in torn jeans (which *would* ruin the appetite), but they shouldn't just be magical forest-boar-mushrooms either. * What if nobody actually knows what the "husks" or "blooms" used to be? The fungus digests whatever it catches—deer, stray dogs, maybe a hiker two years ago—and liquefies it inside a chitinous/fungal shell to grow its own muscle-mycelium. You *can't tell* what it ate to grow that big, and the rule is **you don't ask, and you don't look closely at the vestigial bones in the pelvis when you're jointing the hindquarter.** * That adds a real psychological weight: Bea has to deliberately toss a strangely shaped bone into the stove without letting Simon see it, because they are starving and they *need* to eat. #### 2. Ground the Culinary Process in Gritty Reality (Not Fine Dining) * Instead of comparing the meat to "A5 Wagyu and King Crab," describe it in grounded, tactile terms. When raw, it looks awful—grayish-violet, weeping a clear, sticky sap that smells like wet pennies and rotting sweet-corn. * The discovery shouldn't be a calm scientific theory by Simon. It should be an accident born of misery or housekeeping. Maybe they *have* to burn or boil the chunks on the stove because it's freezing outside and they can't open the door during a spore-squall to dump the body, or they are rendering it down trying to make tallow for lamps/soap. * As it renders in the pot, the penny-smell boils off, and suddenly the kitchen smells like fried chicken skin, browned butter, and roasting marrow. Starving people don't care about "acid denaturing proteins"—they care that their mouths are involuntarily flooding with saliva while standing over a pot of boiled monster. #### 3. Give the Couple Specific, Flawed Humanity * Instead of a picture-perfect homesteading couple, make their dynamic lived-in and slightly frayed. * Maybe Bea wasn't a fancy restaurateur; maybe she ran a mid-tier diner or worked catering, and she has bad knees and a habit of stress-cleaning. Maybe Simon wasn't a park ranger/mycologist; maybe he was an HVAC repairman or a high school shop teacher—someone who knows how to tape up ductwork and rig a deadbolt, not someone with a convenient biology degree. * Give them real starvation symptoms in the beginning: dizziness when standing up, bickering over who used the last match, the weird euphoria and brain-fog of ketosis, clothing hanging off them. #### 4. Mild, Weird Side Effects (Keeping the Edge) * What if eating the spore-meat *is* safe and delicious, and it saves their lives, **but** it has tiny, weird, non-lethal quirks? * Not "turning into zombies," which isn't cozy, but something like: if you eat too much of the marrow, your dreams are ridiculously vivid and shared, or your sweat smells faintly like cinnamon and damp earth, or the monsters outside don't scratch at the doors quite as hard because you smell a little bit like the woods now. It makes their "coziness" slightly uncanny. #### 5. Rethink the Back Half (The Outsider & The Pacing) * Instead of jumping three months ahead to a perfected gourmet paradise with a leather cookbook, keep the timeline tighter, or make their "new normal" feel slightly unhinged. * When the outsider (Devon, or maybe an older, practical neighbor/courier they thought was dead) shows up, the conflict shouldn't lead to an action-movie "Apex Monster Boss Fight." * In cozy-horror, **social tension is scarier and funnier than a giant monster.** What if the climax in Chapters 6–8 is basically a **tense, snowed-in dinner party**? * A massive spore-blizzard traps the visitor inside with Bea and Simon for forty-eight hours. * The visitor is starving, suspicious of why Bea and Simon look so healthy and well-fed when everyone else in the county is dead or eating boiled leather. * The visitor thinks Bea and Simon are hoarders—or worse, cannibals who ate previous travelers! * The climax is the visitor breaking into their locked cellar/smokehouse expecting to find human bodies or stolen FEMA rations, discovering the hanging, butchered spore-fiends, and then a smaller pack of monsters scratching at the cellar bulkhead, forcing the three of them to harvest and cook together while trapped. This "Snowed-in Dinner Party / Misunderstanding" angle for the second half is *much* more human, character-driven, and fitting for a 8,000-word cozy-horror story than an action-movie fight with a "Crowned Goliath." It keeps the focus entirely on the prompt: desperation, the taboo of the food, the domestic warmth of the kitchen, and the bizarre comedy of the situation.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **Core Concept & Genre Balance:** The goal is an 8,000-word cozy-horror short story (~1,000 words per chapter) that feels grounded, tactile, and darkly funny, avoiding sanitized AI tropes. "Cozy" here will not mean a curated Pinterest aesthetic; it will mean the profound physical and emotional **relief** of warmth, full bellies, dry socks, and domestic routine against a bleak, claustrophobic apocalypse. "Horror" will come from the visceral nastiness of the spore-mutants ("Husks"), the psychological taboo of eating something monstrous whose origins you choose not to examine too closely, and the slightly uncanny way the couple adapts to their new diet. **Characters & Voice:** * **POV & Voice:** Third-person limited, tight on **Marge** (early 50s). Marge isn't a Michelin chef; she spent twenty years running the kitchen at a busy highway diner and doing church-basement catering. Her voice is practical, unsentimental, observant, and deeply grounded in the physical mechanics of cooking (rendering fat, scrubbing grease, jointing meat, stretching rations). * **Supporting Cast:** * **Hal** (Marge’s husband, mid-50s): A former county HVAC technician with a bad back. He doesn't have a convenient biology degree; he just knows how to seal ductwork against spores, rig deadbolts, and keep the generator and woodstove running. Their marriage is deeply loving but lived-in—full of shorthand, dark jokes, and the frayed nerves of starvation. * **Toby** (late 20s): A half-starved former postal worker/scavenger who stumbles onto their property in the second half. Instead of an action-movie climax, Toby introduces intense social/psychological tension—suspecting Marge and Hal of being hoarders or cannibals because they are suspiciously well-fed. **The Monsters & Culinary Rules (Aim For & Avoid):** * **Avoid:** Michelin-star buzzwords (*Wagyu, umami symphony, transcendent*), convenient scientific explanations for why the meat is safe, and video-gamey recipes (*Spore-belly bacon*). * **Aim For:** The mutants ("Creeps" or "Bristle-backs") are horrifying amalgamations of mycelium, chitin, and whatever forest biomass (deer, coyotes, maybe an unlucky hiker two years ago—*you don't look closely at the pelvis bones*) the fungus digested to build its ambulatory fruiting body. Raw, they weep a sticky, copper-smelling sap and puff lethal spores. * **The Discovery:** They don't set out to cook it. Trapped indoors during a freeze with a dead Creep in their mudroom, they have to chop it up and burn it in the woodstove so it doesn't rot or release spores. When a chunk hits the hot cast-iron firebox, the copper stench burns off, filling the house with the intoxicating, unmistakable smell of roasting pork shoulder, brown butter, and fried sage. **Pacing & Structure:** Chapters 1–4 cover the grind of starvation, a terrifyingly clumsy break-in by a Creep, the grim chore of disposing of it in the stove, and the desperate, taboo first meal. Chapters 5–8 jump forward six weeks into deep winter: Marge and Hal are thriving (and slightly weird), when Toby arrives during a spore-squall, leading to a tense, claustrophobic "dinner party" where secrets—and recipes—are laid bare. --- # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1: Boiled Rind** * **Scene:** Marge and Hal’s duct-taped ranch house in rural Oregon. Late autumn. Outside, the world is buried in grey drift-mold and the wet, clicking coughs of Creeps in the tree line. * **Beats:** * Establish the physical toll of starvation: the dizziness when standing up, the loose wedding rings, the irritable bickering over a single match, the perpetual chill. * Marge is making "soup" from the boiled, scraped wax-rind of an old cheddar wheel and dried celery flakes. * Hal checks the HVAC plastic sheeting over the windows. A small pack of Creeps shambles past the porch light—blind, multi-limbed things bristling with grey gills and mismatched teeth. Marge and Hal sit in the dark, drinking hot salty water, trying to remember what pot roast tasted like. **Chapter 2: The Mudroom Breach** * **Scene:** Three nights later. A freezing rainstorm drives a solitary, half-frozen Creep against the back of the house. * **Beats:** * The rusted dryer-vent panel in the mudroom gives way. A medium-sized Creep—built like a mangy, six-legged boar fused with rubbery shelf-fungus—squeezes inside, knocking over canning jars. * A clumsy, terrifying, breathless fight in the cramped laundry room. No slick action heroics: Hal gets knocked into the washing machine, his respirator strap twisting, while Marge pins the thing’s snapping head with a snow shovel and hacks at its neck with a heavy butcher’s cleaver until it stops twitching. * They tape the vent shut and bleach the floor, shaking and exhausted. Because a heavy spore-fog is rolling in outside, they can't open the exterior door to drag the two-hundred-pound carcass into the yard. **Chapter 3: Disposal** * **Scene:** The kitchen and mudroom, the next morning. * **Beats:** * The carcass is starting to stiffen and weep a clear, penny-smelling sap. If it blooms in the mudroom, the spores will seep through the door seams. They decide the only safe option is to butcher it into stove-sized chunks and incinerate it piece by piece in the airtight woodstove. * Marge takes over the grim task because she knows how to joint a carcass quickly. As she saws through the outer chitinous rind, she deliberately avoids looking at a disturbingly human-shaped collarbone fused into its ribcage, tossing the bone straight into the ash-bucket. * Beneath the rind, the dense internal "mycelium-meat" is pale violet and marbled with thick, creamy white fat. Hal throws the first heavy slab onto the roaring coals of the stove. * Ten minutes later, the chimney damper leaks a curl of smoke into the living room. It doesn't smell like burning hair or rot. It smells like rendering duck fat, roasted garlic, and Sunday brisket. **Chapter 4: The Taboo** * **Scene:** Beside the woodstove, that afternoon. * **Beats:** * They stand by the stove, mouths flooding with unwanted, painful saliva. They argue about it—Hal thinks they’ve lost their minds from hunger; Marge points out that the heat clearly breaks down the copper-sap, and they have three days of strength left before they can't even haul firewood. * Marge pulls a smaller cut of the violet loin from the butcher's tub. She scrubs her skillet, renders a strip of the creature's white fat, and sears the meat hard with salt and cider vinegar until the purple turns a deep, crusted mahogany. * They feed a thumb-sized piece to the stray mouse they've been trapping in a bucket for weeks. Four hours later, the mouse is fine—fat and grooming its whiskers. * Without speaking, Marge and Hal split the steak. The texture is somewhere between slow-braised oxtail and buttery chanterelles. They eat straight from the skillet with their fingers, weeping quietly from the sheer, violent relief of grease and protein hitting their stomachs. **Chapter 5: Winter Weight** * **Scene:** Six weeks later, mid-winter. The house is snowed in under a thick blanket of white spore-drift. * **Beats:** * The house is warm, smelling of simmering bone-broth and sage. Marge and Hal have put twenty pounds back on. Their skin is healthy, though they've noticed odd little quirks: they sleep ten hours a night with vivid, peaceful dreams, and they never seem to feel the draft anymore. * Hal has modified the mudroom dryer-vent into a deliberate chute-trap baited with warm vinegar rags to lure smaller "Pan-Creeps" right onto the killing floor. * Marge is canning mason jars of potted Creep-meat and rendering tallow for candles. It feels deeply domestic and cozy, until a frantic, human banging sounds at the front storm door. **Chapter 6: The Scavenger** * **Scene:** The living room, evening. * **Beats:** * They let in **Toby**, a frostbitten, gaunt young man in a mildewed postal jacket whose respirator filter is nearly spent. * Marge goes into full diner-hostess mode: stripping off his wet boots, wrapping him in a heated blanket by the stove, and ladling out a mug of golden broth and a plate of shredded, crispy "pot roast" over rehydrated mash. * Toby devours it like a feral dog, stunned by the richness of the food. As the warmth hits him, he starts noticing details: Marge and Hal’s healthy weight, the lack of canned-goods labels in the trash, the heavy padlock on the mudroom door, and a stray, dried chitin-claw Hal accidentally left near the woodbox. **Chapter 7: What's in the Pantry** * **Scene:** The kitchen, late that night. The spore-storm is howling against the plastic-sealed windows. * **Beats:** * Toby doesn't sleep. Convinced that this plump, cheerful older couple lured him in to butcher him like a pig (assuming the "pot roast" was the last traveler who knocked on their door), Toby corners Hal in the kitchen with a fireplace poker, demanding to see what's in the locked mudroom. * Marge comes out in her bathrobe, more annoyed than terrified. Realizing what Toby thinks—that they are cannibals—she is genuinely offended. * She unlocks the mudroom door and turns on the bare bulb, revealing a partially dressed Bristle-back hanging from a gambrel hook over a plastic kiddie pool, next to neat racks of curing sausages. * Before Toby can process the disgust and shock of realizing he just ate two bowls of spore-mutant, the baited chute-trap rattles violently—a fresh Creep has caught the scent of the hanging meat and is wedged halfway through the wall. **Chapter 8: Second Helpings** * **Scene:** The mudroom and kitchen, dawn. * **Beats:** * With Hal’s bad back flared up from the scuffle, Marge hands Toby the snow shovel and barks kitchen-orders at him. Panicked but running on a full stomach for the first time in a year, Toby helps pin the thrashing monster while Marge efficiently dispatches it. * As they bleed and skin the creature together, Marge calmly walks Toby through the anatomy—showing him which glands to cut out, which bones not to look at, and how the loin marbling looks just like pork ribeye once you get past the grey slime. * By sunrise, the storm is clearing. Marge fries up the fresh tenderloin with dried apples and onions for breakfast. * Toby sits at the gingham kitchen table, staring at his fork. His stomach growls. Knowing full well what it is, he takes a bite, closes his eyes, and asks Marge if she has any more of the gravy.

Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Marge Lindqvist **Background, Personality, Idiosyncrasies, Flaws** Marge (53) spent twenty-two years running the back-of-house at *The Pine Cone*, a 24-hour truck stop diner off Highway 97, and supplemented their income catering Lutheran funerals and VFW fish fries. She is unsentimental about food; to her, food isn’t "art," it’s grease, salt, heat, and keeping people upright. * *Idiosyncrasies:* She counts things under her breath when she’s stressed (strokes of a knife sharpener, stitches in a hem). She refuses to waste fat—even before the world ended, she had four coffee cans of categorized bacon and roast drippings under the sink. She wipes counters with the heel of her hand even when she isn't holding a rag. * *Flaws:* She can be aggressively pragmatic to the point of emotional compartmentalization. When she decides not to think about something (like the weird human-looking collarbone inside a Creep), she shuts that mental door with an iron bolt and gets annoyed if Hal tries to pry it open. She also gets mean when her blood sugar drops, resorting to clipped, passive-aggressive kitchen-speak. **Physicality** Built like a fireplug—short, thick-wristed, with heavy forearms scarred from decades of fryer-oil pops and oven racks. At the start of the story, starvation has made her skin hang loose around her jaw and collarbones, which scares her more than the monsters outside because she has never been thin in her life. She wears two pairs of Hal’s wool socks inside broken-in Birkenstocks around the house, moves with an economical waddle to save her bad left meniscus, and always keeps a dish towel tucked into her waistband like a holster. **Motives, Allegiances, Relationships** Her universe begins and ends at the perimeter of her driveway. She and Hal never had kids—just a succession of geriatric labs and thirty years of paying off a 1,200-square-foot ranch house. She loves Hal with a fierce, unromantic loyalty; if he died, she wouldn't bother keeping the woodstove lit. Toward Toby, she feels the instinctive, bossy irritation of a veteran waitress dealing with a wet stray dog tracked into her clean booth—she’ll feed him, dry him off, and put him to work, mostly because watching someone starve in her kitchen insults her pride. **Voice & Flavour Quotes** * *Internal Monologue:* "You don't look at the teeth and you don't look at the pelvis. That’s the rule with hog-butchering when a sow’s gone mean, and it’s the rule here. Once the hide’s off and the silver-skin is trimmed back, meat is just meat, and the skillet doesn't care what it sounded like when it was breathing." * *Dialogue (to Hal, while starving):* "Stop scraping the spoon against the bottom of the bowl, Harold, you aren't going to shave porcelain into broth and it’s setting my teeth on edge." * *Dialogue (to Toby, after he threatens them):* "Oh, put the poker down before you pull a muscle, kid. If I was going to eat a skinny little mailman, I wouldn't have wasted two cups of good gravy fattening you up first. Look at your wrists. You're all gristle." --- # Hal Lindqvist **Background, Personality, Idiosyncrasies, Flaws** Hal (56) worked twenty-eight years for Deschutes County Facilities & HVAC before the spores blew in from the coast. He is the kind of rural handy-man who owns seven coffee tins full of rusted washers "just in case," knows how to bypass a dead circuit board with a paperclip, and reads installation manuals on the toilet for fun. * *Idiosyncrasies:* He sniffs the air constantly—an old HVAC habit from hunting freon leaks and dead mice in return ducts. He talks to inanimate objects when fixing them ("Come on now, sweetheart, don't strip on me"). Since they started eating the Creeps, he’s developed a habit of humming low, rhythmic, three-note tunes he doesn't realize he's humming until Marge pokes him. * *Flaws:* He is a worrier who masks it behind folksy understatement. Unlike Marge, who can turn off her imagination while cutting meat, Hal overthinks the morality and biology of what they’re doing, leading him to procrastinate on chores around the kill-chute. He is also stubborn about his physical decline, refusing to admit his L4-L5 disc is blown out until his legs literally give way. **Physicality** Tall, slope-shouldered, with a classic mechanic’s build: skinny legs, a former beer belly that initially deflated into a sad apron of skin, and huge, permanently grease-stained knuckles with flat, split thumbnails. He has a greying walrus mustache that he trims with Marge’s sewing scissors (much to her fury) and wears a faded quilted flannel shirt with duct tape over the left elbow to keep the batting from falling out. When his back hurts, he stands with one hand braced against his kidney like an old teapot. **Motives, Allegiances, Relationships** Hal’s greatest terror isn't being torn apart by a Bristle-back; it’s his own body failing him while Marge still needs heavy things lifted. He views the house as a life-support machine he is personally responsible for keeping pressurized and warm. He adores Marge and relies entirely on her blunt common sense to keep him from spiraling into existential dread. When Toby arrives, Hal is genuinely thrilled just to talk to another guy about the weather and road conditions, completely oblivious at first to how creepy he and Marge seem to an outsider. **Voice & Flavour Quotes** * *Internal Monologue:* "The secret to keeping the drift-mold out of a crawlspace wasn't fancy military filters; it was six-milvisqueen sheeting, three cases of Nashua foil tape, and not thinking too hard about what was scratching against the cinderblocks three feet under the linoleum." * *Dialogue (when the meat first hits the stove):* "Marge... I’m not saying we oughta get a fork. I’m just saying, if the good Lord didn't want us wondering about it, He shouldn't have made the damn thing smell like the Kiwanis Club pancake breakfast." * *Dialogue (to Toby):* "Well, sure, the first couple weeks you get the night-sweats a little, and your dreams get real colorful—lots of trees talking to each other and whatnot—but hell, beats waking up at three in the morning with your stomach eating your backbone." --- # Toby Vance **Background, Personality, Idiosyncrasies, Flaws** Toby (27) was a rural route carrier for the USPS for three years before the collapse. He survived fourteen months longer than most people in the county because he knew every backroad, hunting cabin, and prepper’s root cellar between Bend and La Pine, and because he is a world-class coward who runs at the first sign of a spore-cloud. * *Idiosyncrasies:* He still checks his Casio wristwatch every ten minutes even though the battery died in October. He hoards packets of fast-food condiments in his pockets (dried-out soy sauce, crusty ketchup packets) and sucks on the foil corners when he walks. He flinches at loud metallic clangs. * *Flaws:* Deeply paranoid, twitchy, and judgmental in the way only someone who has been starving and alone for a year can be. He has read too many post-apocalyptic paperbacks and immediately assumes that anyone doing well in the wasteland must be a sadistic warlord or a cannibal. He is also terrible with his hands—he couldn't skin a rabbit or fix a carburetor to save his life. **Physicality** Wiry and hollowed-out. Six feet tall and weighing maybe a hundred and twenty-five pounds soaking wet. His skin has the grey, waxy sheen of someone living on multi-vitamins and lard, with purple frost-nip scars on the tips of his ears and nose. He wears a stiff, salt-stained USPS windbreaker layered over three stolen sweaters, and his eyes are constantly darting toward exits and heavy blunt objects. Once he gets food in him, his whole body goes slack and sleepy like an overfed puppy. **Motives, Allegiances, Relationships** At first, Toby just wants to not freeze to death before Tuesday. He has no grand hope of rebuilding society; he just wants his feet to stop hurting and his belly to stop cramping. He initially views Marge and Hal as potential predators wearing a "grandma and grandpa" disguise, then as absolute lunatics when he sees the butchered Creep, and finally—with the pragmatism of the truly desperate—as the best thing that ever happened to him. **Voice & Flavour Quotes** * *Internal Monologue:* "Nobody has cheeks that pink in January unless they’re eating meat every day, and there hasn't been a live cow in Deschutes County since the spring bloom. Which meant whatever was in that brown gravy was either the neighbors’ golden retriever or the neighbors themselves." * *Dialogue (panicking in the kitchen):* "Stay back by the fridge! I’m serious, mister, I’ll stove your head in! I saw the boot-pile by the basement door—who’d those belong to, huh? Who’s in the jars?!" * *Dialogue (the morning after, staring at his plate):* "Wait. So the little crunchy bits you fried up with the onions... those aren't cracklings? Those are the—okay, no, don't tell me. Just pass the pepper."

Model Output:
Marge stood at the stove, scraping a paring knife across a brick of red wax that had once held two pounds of Tillamook sharp cheddar. *One, two, three, four.* She counted the strokes under her breath, angling the blade so the tiny, yellowed curls of cheese clinging to the inside of the paraffin fell into the saucepan. She had already boiled the wax twice this week, fishing it out with a slotted spoon before it could melt entirely and ruin the pot, though at this point she wasn't sure what she was saving the Revere Ware for. "Quit hovering, Harold," she said without turning around. "You're blocking the light from the lantern, and my eyes are bad enough." Hal shifted his weight off his left hip, the linoleum creaking under his wool socks. He had his right hand braced against his lower back like an old teapot, his thumb hooked into the belt loop of jeans that had belonged to him for ten years and now hung off his tailbone in sad, pleated folds. "Wasn't hovering. Was checking the seal on the transom window. Draft's coming through somewhere." "There's no draft. You checked it at four." "Well, my neck's cold." "Your neck's cold because you've got no meat on your collarbones anymore," Marge said. She flicked the last curl of waxy cheese off her thumb into the water, shook three dried celery flakes out of a spice tin whose label had peeled off during the Carter administration, and gave the whole miserable business a stir. "Go sit by the firebox. It'll be boiling in a minute." Hal didn't go sit. He lingered by the kitchen sink, sniffing the air—two short, sharp inhales through his mustache, the same way he used to hunt for freon leaks or dead packrats in the county courthouse return ducts. Across the double-paned glass above the faucets, six-mil plastic sheeting was taped down with silver Nashua foil tape, turning the twilight outside into a blurry, bruised smear of purple and slate grey. You couldn't see the Ponderosas across the gravel turnaround anymore, just the fuzzy silhouettes of the drift-mold that had swallowed the lower branches up to twelve feet. When the wind came down off the Cascades, the mold didn't rustle like pine needles; it made a heavy, wet *shuck-shuck* sound, like somebody turning over a tarp full of soaked laundry. "There's three of 'em out by the propane tank," Hal said quietly. Marge didn't look up from the burner. "Big ones?" "Medium. Bristle-backs, looks like. One's got a bum leg, dragging its hindquarters through the gravel. Snuffling around the regulator." "They can snuffle all they want. Tank's been dry since August." Marge reached into her apron pocket to adjust her wedding band. She had wrapped forty turns of white quilting thread around the bottom of the gold band back in October to keep it from sliding over her knuckle into the dishwater, and now even the thread was loose. She wiped the clean Formica counter with the heel of her hand, a phantom swipe that caught nothing. "Turn the porch bulb off, Hal. No sense running the battery down just to watch 'em drool." Hal clicked the wall switch down. Outside, in the sudden dark beyond the plastic, something let out a long, rattling sigh—like a bellows wheezing through wet gravel—followed by the sharp, rhythmic *clack-clack-clack* of chitinous teeth snapping against the iron lid of the propane pig. Marge poured the boiling water into two heavy ceramic mugs from *The Pine Cone*. The diner had burned down fourteen months ago, right around the time the National Guard cordoned off Highway 97 and found out the hard way that canister filters didn't stop the yellow spores once the fruiting bodies started popping in the ditches. Marge had stolen a dozen mugs from the dish pit on her last shift, along with five gallons of fry oil and a thirty-pound lug of russet potatoes. The oil and the potatoes had lasted till May. The canned peaches and deer jerky in the crawlspace had lasted till September. Now it was November, and they were drinking hot salty water that smelled vaguely of wax candles and old celery. She carried the mugs into the living room and set them on the hearthstones in front of the Blaze King woodstove. They had closed off the two bedrooms and the hallway with stapled moving blankets to keep the heat in the main room, dragging their mattress down onto the braided rug. Hal eased himself down onto the edge of the mattress with a groan that rattled in his chest, taking his mug between both large, grease-stained hands. His thumbnails were split down the middle, and his skin had that translucent, papery look Marge remembered from church-basement visitation hours when the cancer patients finally came home on hospice. She sat beside him on a flipped-over five-gallon pickle bucket, blowing across the surface of her mug. A single silver curl of fat—no wider than an eyelash—floated on top. "Remember that chuck roast I did for your brother's fiftieth?" Marge said after a minute, staring at the orange glow behind the stove's mica window. Hal took a tiny sip and winced as the scalding water hit his tongue. "The one with the little white onions?" "Pearl onions. Took me forty minutes to peel four pounds of those little bastards. Dredged the beef in flour and paprika, browned it in two inches of bacon grease in the big roasting pan until the fond on the bottom was black as tar, then deglazed it with two bottles of that dark beer Gary brought down from Hood River." Hal closed his eyes. Under his mustache, his jaw worked slightly. "Had carrots in it." "Big chunks. Cut on the bias so they wouldn't go mushy. You ate four slabs of it and fell asleep in the lawn chair with your plate on your belly, and the lab licked the gravy right off your shirt." "Good dog," Hal murmured. "Good gravy, too." He lifted his mug again, tilting it all the way back, then used the tip of his spoon to chase the three soggy flecks of celery around the bottom. The metal rasped loudly against the stoneware. *Scritch. Scritch.* "Stop scraping the spoon against the bottom of the bowl, Harold," Marge snapped, a sudden, hot wire of fury tightening behind her eyeballs. "You aren't going to shave porcelain into broth and it's setting my teeth on edge." Hal's hand froze. For a second, his face crumpled—not angry, just tired in a way that made him look seventy instead of fifty-six. He set the mug down on the hearthstone without a word. Marge squeezed her eyes shut. Her heart was hammering a fast, thin beat against her ribs, the way it always did lately when she stood up too fast or yelled. "I'm sorry," she whispered, reaching out to lay her broad, scarred hand over his knobby knee. "My head's light." "I know, honey," Hal said softly, patting her knuckles. Outside, near the corner of the house by the laundry room, gravel crunched under something heavy, and dry gills scraped along the aluminum siding like a rake over tin. Hal sighed, his stomach giving a long, hollow gurgle that echoed in the quiet room. "I know."

Three nights later, the sky opened up and dropped two inches of freezing slush on top of the drift-mold, and the cold drove the Creeps against the foundation. Marge woke at two in the morning to the sound of galvanized tin tearing like wet cardboard. She didn't sit up—sitting up too fast made the black spots dance behind her eyes—so she rolled off the mattress onto her hands and knees first, pushing herself up by the edge of the pickle bucket. On the other side of the rug, Hal was already upright, fumbling his grey rubber half-mask respirator over his nose with shaking fingers. *Clang.* A jar of buttons she kept on the mudroom dryer hit the linoleum and exploded. "The vent," Hal wheezed, his voice muffled and tinny through the pink Honeywell cartridges. He yanked the elastic strap over his crown, tangling it in his thinning hair so his left ear folded down at a painful angle. "The four-inch exhaust pipe. Rust finally gave out." Marge jammed her own mask over her face, the cold silicone sucking tight against her hollow cheeks as she blew out hard to check the seal. Her slippers were by the stove, so she didn't bother with shoes, just grabbed the heavy fourteen-inch Dexter butcher's cleaver she kept wedged between the kindling box and the wall. Hal had his boar-spear—an eight-foot pine closet rod with a lawnmower blade bolted and wire-wrapped to the end. The mudroom door was hollow-core Lauan plywood, and by the time Hal threw the brass deadbolt back, something was already thumping against the lower panel like a sack of wet concrete dropped from a tailgate. Hal kicked the door inward and clicked on his headband flashlight. The beam cut through a swirling fog of yellow dust and insulation batting. Wedged two-thirds of the way through the blown-out plywood patch behind the Maytag was a Creep the size of a yearling hog. It wasn't one of the tall, spindly ones that clicked in the tree line; this was a burrower, thick and low-slung, its back plated in overlapping shingles of grey, rubbery shelf-fungus that glistened with freezing rain. Six jointed legs—four like a coyote's, two thicker ones near the chest that looked entirely too much like skinned forearms—scrabbled wildly for traction against the spilled Tide powder and broken Mason jars on the floor. As the light hit it, the thing split its head down the middle. It didn't have a jaw so much as three vertical petals of pale, fibrous cartilage lined with mismatched rows of flat deer-molars and yellow canine fangs, all of them snapping shut with a wet, hollow *clop* that sprayed stringy clear sap across the washing machine. "Pin it!" Marge barked through her respirator. "Don't let it get its hind feet under the dryer!" Hal lunged forward, driving the lawnmower blade into the thick crease where the thing's neck met its fungal mantle. Five years ago, Hal could have lifted a two-hundred-pound compressor into the back of his F-250 by himself. Now, his arms trembled like wet reeds, and the blade skittered off the tough, leathery rind, only biting an inch deep into the purple flesh beneath. The Creep shrieked—a high, whistling wheeze through the gill-slits along its ribs, puffing a cloud of rust-colored spores straight into the flashlight beam—and jerked sideways. The pine closet rod snapped in half against the edge of the utility sink. Hal's wool socks hit the slick Tide powder and went out from under him. He went down hard, the back of his head bouncing off the front of the Maytag with a hollow *thump* that knocked his headlamp cockeyed, shining the beam straight up at the water heater. "Hal!" The Creep scrambled entirely free of the wall, trailing shreds of pink fiberglass insulation from its spines. It scrambled over Hal's outstretched legs, its front claws gouging long white tracks in the linoleum as its three-part maw snapped an inch from his flannel collar. Hal had both hands wedged under its throat, trying to lever the snapping teeth away from his respirator hose, his back arched and his boots kicking uselessly against the baseboard. Marge didn't think about her bad knee. She grabbed the red plastic snow shovel standing by the freezer, stepped over Hal's shin, and jammed the steel wear-strip of the shovel blade straight down across the thing's snout, pinning the lower petal of its jaw to the laundry room floor. She put her whole weight on the shovel handle, bracing her chest against the grip while the creature thrashed and whipped its heavy hindquarters against the drywall, denting the plaster. With her right hand, she raised the Dexter cleaver and brought it down. *One.* The heavy carbon-steel blade bit through the grey shelf-fungus behind the skull with a sound like splitting a green squash. Thick, copper-smelling sap spurted over her bare wrists. *Two. Three. Four.* She hacked into the same notch, counting the strokes, her breath whistling raggedly through the pink filter cartridges until her shoulder socket burned and the blade hit the linoleum underneath with a dull *thunk*. The six legs gave a violent, synchronized jerk that knocked the washing machine two inches off its leveling feet, and then the gills along its flanks collapsed with a long, wet hiss, like an inner tube going flat. For a full minute, nobody moved. The only sound in the twelve-by-six room was the rattle of Marge's breathing in her mask and the slow *drip-drip-drip* of clear violet-tinted fluid running off the edge of the dryer. "You got a puncture?" Marge gasped, her knees trembling so hard her heels hammered the floor. "No," Hal breathed from under the carcass's front legs. His voice was high and tight. "Seal's good. My back—Jesus, Marge, my back's locked up, I can't roll it off me." Marge dropped the cleaver, grabbed the thing by two of its rigid dorsal plates, and hauled backward with everything she had left in her hips. The body was dead weight, dense and surprisingly warm through the cold slime on its hide, like a fresh-killed pig before the scald. It rolled off Hal's thighs with a heavy slap. She didn't help Hal up first; she couldn't afford to. Cold night air and grey drift-spores were pouring through the ragged hole behind the dryer. Working with furious, practiced speed, Marge shoved a bundled wool army blanket into the breach, dragged a leftover sheet of four-mil plastic over the whole wall, and ran six strips of silver foil tape around the edges, pressing the adhesive flat with the heel of her hand. Only once the plastic stopped billowing did she grab the jug of Clorox by the sink, uncap it with her teeth, and splash half a gallon of straight bleach over the carcass, the floor, and the front of Hal's jeans. The chemical fumes rose up thick and blinding, stinging their eyes even above the rubber masks, cutting through the sharp, metallic reek of the dead Creep. Marge dropped to her knees beside the washing machine, hooking her hands under Hal's armpits to drag him back toward the kitchen door, leaving the two-hundred-pound thing sprawling across the threshold in a widening puddle of bleach and sap.

By eight the next morning, the Creep had started to stiffen up, and the mudroom smelled like a bucket of wet pennies left out in the sun. Hal sat backward on one of the kitchen dinette chairs with a hot towel pressed against his lower spine, watching through the doorway as Marge poked the carcass with the broom handle. They still had their respirators strapped on, though they had taken the cartridges off for twenty minutes at dawn to sip cold cistern water under the blanket tent in the living room. "We can't drag it out the back," Hal said, his voice muffled through the grey rubber. "Barometer's down to twenty-nine. Fog's so thick out there I can't even see the woodshed, and there's two more of 'em clicking down by the culvert. We crack that exterior seal now, we'll have the whole county in here." "Well, it can't stay on the linoleum," Marge said. She prodded the grey shelf-fungus along the thing's spine. Where the bleach had splashed it, the rubbery plates had turned a chalky, blistered white, like scalded tripe, and the little spore-gills underneath were fused shut. "When they go rigor like this, they pop within twenty-four hours. Remember that deer-thing that died in the ditch in July? Puffed up like a wood tick and blew yellow dust all over the windshield." "Could wrap it in visqueen. Tape the seams." "It'll rot right through the tape, Harold, and then we got two hundred pounds of liquid mushroom fermenting ten feet from the bed." Marge looked back over her shoulder at the living room, where the Blaze King was ticking softly, damped down over a bed of lodgepole pine coals. "Door on the firebox is fourteen by sixteen. If I joint it down small enough, we can burn it." Hal blinked at her over the bridge of his mask. "Burn it? In the house?" "It's an airtight stove, Hal. Catalytic combustor's still good, isn't it? Once the draft's roaring, everything goes straight up the flue at nine hundred degrees. We do it a chunk at a time so we don't choke the coals." Hal rubbed his temple, wincing as he shifted his weight. "I don't know if I can bend over to help you saw it up, honey. Disc is pinching the nerve something fierce. Left foot's numb to the ankle." "I don't need you hovering in the doorway anyway. I broke down forty-pound cases of frozen pork butts by myself for twenty years while the dishwasher was out back smoking dope," Marge said, already reaching for her blue rubber dish gloves under the sink. "Go stoke the stove. Get it hot enough to turn the stovepipe cherry. And bring me the galvanized washtub from under the porch stairs." It took her forty minutes to get the outer rind off. She worked on her knees on a folded tarp, usingHal's Stanley utility knife to score down the belly-seam and her six-inch Victorinox boning knife to peel the heavy, chitinous plates back from the ribs. She didn't let herself think about what the thing had looked like when it was snapping at Hal's throat. Once the three-petaled head was severed and shoved straight into a double-bagged Hefty sack with a cup of bleach, it wasn't a monster anymore. It was just a carcass that hadn't been bled right. You don't look at the teeth, and you don't look at the pelvis. That was the rule. Halfway through parting the front shoulder joint, the tip of her boning knife hit something hard and strangely curved buried inside the grey collar-gristle. It wasn't a deer bone, and it wasn't a coyote's. It had the distinct, shallow S-curve of a human clavicle, fused seamless and pale into a cage of calcified mycelium. Marge didn't pause. She didn't look toward the kitchen door to see if Hal was watching. She wedged the Dexter cleaver into the notch behind the bone, snapped it free with one sharp pop of her palm, and dropped it straight into the covered ash-bucket beside her knee, burying it under two inches of cold grey wood-ash. *One, two, three, four.* She wiped her gloved hands on her apron and kept cutting. Once the outer rind and the grey gill-flaps were stripped away, the inside of the Creep didn't look like rot at all. There were no guts to speak of—no stomach sack or green tripe to puncture and foul the meat, just a central cord of fibrous white root-matter running from throat to tail. And packed around that cord were thick, heavy muscles of dense violet flesh, the color of a fresh-sliced eggplant, marbled all the way through with veins of firm, creamy white fat. As she sliced a four-pound slab off the backstrap to fit the stove door, the penny smell faded entirely. The newly exposed meat didn't weep sap. It was dry and tacky to the touch, like aged beef hanging in a walk-in cooler, and through the thin edge of her respirator where the strap was loose by her cheek, she caught a faint, sweet whiff that made her knife-hand stall. It smelled like raw hazelnuts and sweet cream butter. "Fire's up," Hal called from the living room, shuffling back in with the poker for a cane. "Damper's wide open. Bring a piece in, let's see if it smokes." Marge carried the galvanized tub in by one handle, her left knee clicking softly on the threshold. Hal swung the heavy cast-iron stove door open. A wave of dry, blistering heat washed over their faces. Using the long iron tongs, Marge lifted the four-pound chunk of violet loin and shoved it straight onto the white-hot pine coals at the back of the firebox, slamming the latch shut before the sap could hiss. Through the mica glass, the edges of the meat curled instantly. The white fat began to bubble and run, dripping down into the glowing ash with sharp, yellow flares of flame. For five minutes, they stood side by side in the dim room, watching it char. Then the catalytic damper above the collar gave a little heat-tick, and a thin, invisible ribbon of draft blew back through the air-intake lever at the bottom of the door. Hal pulled his respirator down off his nose first. He did his HVAC sniff—two short, sharp inhales. Then he did it again, deeper, his eyes widening behind his smudged glasses. Marge pulled her own mask down around her neck. The living room didn't smell like burning hair, or bleach, or hot copper pennies. It smelled like the back kitchen of *The Pine Cone* at five-thirty on a Sunday morning when the cured hams came out of the alto-shaam and the grill cook dropped a pound of chopped sage and onions into the dripping pan. It was a rich, heavy, savory cloud of browned fat, caramelized crust, and roasted bone marrow that hung in the warm air by the ceiling. Under her wool sweater, Marge's empty stomach contracted so violently she had to brace a hand against the mantel to keep from doubling over. Her mouth flooded with hot, sharp saliva that actually hurt the glands under her jaw. Hal stared at the little mica window, where the purple slab had turned a deep, crackling mahogany brown, bubbling in its own clear grease. "Marge," Hal whispered, his voice cracking down the middle. "I'm not saying we oughta get a fork. I'm just saying, if the good Lord didn't want us wondering about it, He shouldn't have made the damn thing smell like the Kiwanis Club pancake breakfast."

"You're out of your mind," Hal said twenty minutes later, though he hadn't moved an inch from the hearthstones and his eyes were glued to the galvanized tub on the kitchen floor. "It's the ketosis talking. Read about it in *Field & Stream* once. Guys trapped in a line cabin up in the Yukon start looking at their own snowshoes like they're T-bones." "Snowshoes don't marble like a prime ribeye, Harold," Marge said. Her voice was flat and brisk, the tone she used when the health inspector showed up during the lunch rush. She was at the counter with her ten-inch Griswold cast-iron skillet, scrubbing the cold surface with coarse kosher salt and a dry rag. "And I'm not hallucinating the grease coming off that damper. My nose works fine." "It's a spore-thing, Marge! One puff of that yellow dust out in the ditch turns your lungs into cauliflower in six hours!" "And if you eat raw giant morels out of the burn-scar up by Sisters, you'll shit your insides out till your heart stops," Marge shot back, turning around with her hands on her hips. "You boil 'em or fry 'em in butter for ten minutes, they go for forty dollars a pound at the farmers' market in Bend. Heat changes things. Acid changes things. You saw what the bleach did to the gills out there—melted 'em flat." Hal swallowed hard. His Adam's apple bobbed up and down in the hollow column of his throat like a cork in a bottle. "We got that half-sack of lawn seed in the shed. Once the fog clears tomorrow, I could try boiling the fescue—" "You can't walk to the toilet without leaning on a broomstick, Hal!" Marge's voice cracked, sharp and loud in the low-ceilinged kitchen. She looked down at her own forearm, where the pale skin draped over the radius bone like wet tissue paper. "We got maybe four days left before neither one of us has the leg-strength to haul split pine in from the porch. Once the fire goes out, we freeze in two hours. I would rather choke to death on a hot piece of whatever that is than lie under six blankets for a week listening to you shiver." Hal opened his mouth, closed it, and looked down at his split thumbnails. He didn't argue anymore. Marge didn't take the chunk out of the woodstove—that one had pine-ash crusted to the bottom. Instead, she put her blue rubber gloves back on, reached into the galvanized tub, and lifted out the clean center-cut of the backstrap she'd trimmed earlier. It weighed about two pounds, cold and dense in her palm. She trimmed off a long ribbon of the creamy white fat from the outer edge and dropped it into the dry skillet over the stove's flat cast-iron top-plate, where the heat was fiercest. It didn't sizzle right away. For ten seconds, it gave off a faint, sharp hiss that smelled briefly of copper and damp basement walls. Marge held her breath, her hand hovering over the respirator hanging around her neck. Then the fat melted into a clear, golden liquid, and the copper smell vanished—snapped out of existence like a blown match. The kitchen filled with a nutty, rich aroma that smelled like rendered duck fat and toasted filberts. Marge unstoppered the green glass bottle by the salt pig and poured two tablespoons of Bragg's apple cider vinegar over the raw violet meat in a pie tin, turning it twice before patting it dry with a clean flour-sack towel. Wherever the vinegar touched the purple fibers, they paled to the color of raw veal. She salted it heavily, ground black pepper over both sides—*one, two, three, four*—and laid the loin into the smoking skillet. The sear was loud and violent, throwing tiny, clear beads of hot oil against her knuckles. She didn't flinch. Those grease-pops felt like home. She cooked it twelve minutes on a side, basting the top with a soupspoon until the outside formed a thick, mahogany crust that crackled under the bowl of the spoon and the center felt firm as a flexed thumb-pad—well past medium-well, pushing two hundred degrees internal. If anything was still alive in that mycelium, it was tougher than God. When she lifted it onto a warm stoneware platter to rest, she sliced off a corner the size of her pinky nail, blew on it until it was lukewarm, and walked over to the pantry closet. Inside, at the bottom of a tall five-gallon drywall bucket with a greased ramp leading up the side, sat the white-footed deer mouse Hal had caught chewing on the candle stubs three days ago. They'd been saving him, though neither of them had said out loud what for. Marge dropped the browned scrap into the bucket. The mouse didn't hesitate. It darted across the plastic, grabbed the meat in both front paws, and ate the whole thing in thirty seconds flat, including licking the grease spot off the bucket floor. "Now we wait," Marge said, setting the platter on the back corner of the stove behind an overturned stockpot to keep it warm. Those four hours were the longest afternoon of their thirty-one years together. They didn't play cribbage because their hands shook too hard to peg the board, and they Couldn't sleep because the smell leaking out from under the stockpot was a physical torture. Hal got up every twenty minutes to peer down into the drywall bucket with his headlamp. At five o'clock, the mouse was curled in a ball of shredded newspaper at the bottom of the pail, fat-bellied, grooming its ears with brisk, tidy swipes of its front paws, its black eyes bright as shoe-buttons. Marge didn't ask Hal if he was ready. She took the stockpot off the platter, set the Griswold skillet back on the hot plate for sixty seconds to get the drippings bubbling again, and sliced the rested loin into half-inch medallions. Inside the dark crust, the meat was the pale, pearlescent ivory of roasted pork loin, glistening with clear juices that pooled in the well of the platter. She didn't bother with plates or forks. She carried the platter straight to the mattress by the firebox, sat down beside Hal, and handed him a thick center slice between two fingers. Hal looked at it. Then he looked at Marge. With his free hand, he reached out and hooked his pinky around the loose belt of her bathrobe. They bit down at the same time. The crust shattered between Marge's molars—salty, crisp, and sharp with black pepper and vinegar. Beneath it, the meat didn't chew like mushroom at all; it had the long, tender grain of a ten-hour braised oxtail, giving way instantly into a buttery, velvet richness that coated the roof of her mouth and the back of her throat in warm fat. There was no metallic tang, no dirt, no rot—just a deep, woodsy sweetness underneath the savoriness, like chestnuts roasted in beef tallow. Hal made a low, strangled sound in his throat. Before she had finished swallowing the first mouthful, Marge had a second slice halfway to her teeth. They didn't talk. They didn't chew twenty times like polite company. They ate hunched over the platter between their knees, grease running down their chins and dripping onto their wool socks, licking the salt and browned fond off their knuckles with rough, frantic tongues. Halfway through the last piece, Marge realized her face was wet. She wasn't sobbing; the tears were just leaking steadily out of the corners of her eyes, hot and salty, mixing with the butter-fat on her upper lip as the first real wave of heat hit the bottom of her stomach and radiated outward to the tips of her freezing fingers. When the platter was empty, Hal took his crooked forefinger, wiped the last smear of brown jelly from the porcelain ridge, and sucked it clean. He leaned his head back against the brick hearth, his chest rising and falling in deep, wet breaths. "We got about forty pounds of meat left in that tub in the kitchen, Marge," he whispered. Marge wiped her mouth with the dish towel tucked in her waist, her heart beating a slow, heavy, solid thump against her ribs for the first time since July. "Fifty," she said. "If I render the belly flaps."

[Analysis] Chapter 4 is a remarkably accomplished piece of genre-blending fiction that largely delivers on the ambitious plan laid out in the writing intention. The detail that she "didn't flinch" at grease pops because they "felt like home" is quietly devastating and perfectly in character. Her argument with Hal—invoking morels and the farmers' market in Bend—is exactly the kind of unsentimental, practical reasoning the character profile demands. She doesn't moralize; she problem-solves. Hal is also well-rendered. His Field & Stream reference, his snowshoe-as-T-bone anecdote, his Adam's apple bobbing "like a cork in a bottle," his folksy understatement masking genuine terror—all consistent with the profile. His final whispered line about the forty pounds of meat is perfectly calibrated: the worrier who has accepted the situation and is already calculating forward. The mouse as a proxy taster is a brilliant narrative device—practical, darkly funny, and entirely in keeping with Marge's character. It avoids the convenient "scientific explanation" the plan warned against while still providing a plausible in-world justification. **Prose Quality** The prose is largely excellent. The cooking sequence is the standout: technically grounded, sensory without being overwrought, and paced with the rhythm of someone who actually knows how to cook. "Wherever the vinegar touched the purple fibers, they paled to the color of raw veal" is precise and evocative without being purple. The sear described as "loud and violent, throwing tiny, clear beads of hot oil against her knuckles" is viscerally accurate. The eating scene is the emotional climax and it earns its sentiment. "The crust shattered between Marge's molars" through to the tears "mixing with the butter-fat on her upper lip" is genuinely moving—the relief is physical and the emotion is conveyed through physical detail rather than stated. The plan called for them to "weep quietly from the sheer, violent relief of grease and protein hitting their stomachs" and the execution honors that intention without melodrama. **Weaknesses and Criticisms** There are a few stumbles. "His Adam's apple bobbed up and down in the hollow column of his throat like a cork in a bottle" is slightly overwrought—the simile is functional but the "hollow column" phrasing is a touch purple. The phrase "tougher than God" is a bit of a cliché. "Bright as shoe-buttons" for the mouse's eyes is a well-worn comparison. The capitalization error ("they Couldn't sleep") is a minor copyediting flaw that shouldn't be in polished work. The four-hour waiting period is handled efficiently but the line "Those four hours were the longest afternoon of their thirty-one years together" is the one moment where the prose tells rather than shows—it's a statement of emotional weight rather than an earned demonstration of it. The subsequent details (shaking hands, Hal checking the bucket every twenty minutes) partially recover this, but the declarative sentence is a slight lapse. The description of the meat's flavor—"like chestnuts roasted in beef tallow"—is good, but the overall flavor description, while restrained compared to what it could have been, still leans slightly toward the "food writing" register the plan warned against. It stays on the right side of the line, but barely. **Plot and Structure** The chapter follows the plan faithfully: the argument, the cooking process, the mouse test, the four-hour wait, the meal. The beats are hit in order and with appropriate weight. The final exchange—"Fifty, if I render the belly flaps"—is a perfect closing line: darkly funny, character-consistent, and forward-looking without being saccharine. **Tonal Balance** The cozy-horror balance is well-maintained. The horror is present in the violet meat, the copper smell, the deliberate avoidance of examining the creature's origins, and the taboo of the act itself. The coziness is in the cast-iron skillet, the kosher salt, the dish towel, the mattress by the firebox. Neither overwhelms the other. **Overall Assessment** This is a high-quality chapter that executes its plan with skill, maintains character voice consistently, and achieves genuine emotional resonance through physical specificity rather than sentimentality. The flaws are minor: a few worn similes, one tell-don't-show lapse, one copyediting error. It is not a masterpiece—the prose occasionally reaches for effect rather than earning it—but it is very good work. By the second week of January, the drift-mold outside had frozen into four-foot grey hummocks that looked like dirty sheep huddled against the fence posts, and Marge had had to let the waistband of her wool skirt out an inch and a half. She stood at the kitchen counter in a pair of Hal's thick rag socks—just one pair now, her feet stayed plenty warm on their own—packing cubed shoulder-meat into wide-mouth Ball jars. Into each pint she dropped half a bay leaf from the coffee can on the windowsill, a quarter-teaspoon of kosher salt, and two whole peppercorns, then ladled boiling white tallow up to the neck line before wiping the rim with a vinegar rag. *One, two, three, four.* She spun the brass bands down tight with a flick of her thick wrist and lowered them into the speckled blue pressure canner sitting over the Blaze King's top plate. The house didn't smell like wet pennies or bleach anymore. It smelled like a butcher shop in December: rendered lard, bay laurel, woodsmoke, and the rich, dark broth that had been simmering at the back of the stove in an eight-quart stockpot for six days straight. In the mudroom, the circular saw whined through a piece of two-by-six fir, followed by the rhythmic *thwack-thwack* of Hal's framing hammer. A moment later, the mudroom door swung open and Hal came in, brushing sawdust off his flannel belly. The grey, papery pleats around his jaw had filled back out to a ruddy pink, and the dark hollows under his eyes were gone. He wasn't leaning on the broomstick anymore, either, though he still kept his palm braced against his kidney when he stood up from a squat. As he walked to the sink to wash his hands, he was humming under his breath—that same low, three-note tune he'd been humming since New Year's, slow and steady like a chord on a pump organ. "Quit humming that, Harold," Marge said pleasantly, adjusting the brass weight on the canner vent. "You sound like a refrigerator with a bad compressor." Hal blinked, stopping with the bar of Lava soap in his hands. "Was I doing it again?" "Since breakfast. How's the chute?" "Slicker'n snot on a brass doorknob," Hal said proudly, drying his knuckles on a flour towel. He had pulled the broken Maytag dryer away from the back wall three weeks ago and replaced the rusted four-inch exhaust pipe with an eighteen-inch square culvert he'd salvaged out of his shop—sheet-metal lined, angled slightly downward onto a greased sheet of corrugated roofing tin, with a drop-gate made from an old cast-iron tractor weight rigged to a tripwire inside the laundry room. "Hung a rag soaked in warm bacon grease and apple vinegar right inside the outer flap. Next time a little pan-Creep comes snuffling through the drift after dark, he'll slide right in up to his hips and the weight'll drop behind his ears. Won't even have to put my boots on." "Just don't bait it till Thursday," Marge said, wiping the clean Formica with the heel of her hand. "I still got twelve pints of the last one to process, and the curing rack behind the water heater's full of links. Where'd you put the tallow candles?" "In the milk crate by the woodbox." Hal walked over behind her, hooked his chin over her shoulder, and sniffed the steam rising around the canner lid. "You sleeping okay, honey? You were twitching your feet again around four." "I wasn't twitching. I was dreaming about the Ponderosas up by Crescent Lake," Marge said. She didn't mention that in the dream she hadn't been looking at the trees; she had been forty feet underground, feeling the cold water trickle over her toes while she traded slow, polite chemical clicks with every spruce root between here and Klamath Falls. It was a very restful sort of dream, much nicer than the ones she used to have about dropping thirty plates of country-fried steak during the Sunday church rush, and when she woke up, her left knee didn't ache at all. "Go throw another split on the fire. Gauge needs to hit ten pounds and stay there for ninety minutes." Hal turned toward the living room, reaching for the split-pine box on the hearth. Before his fingers touched the bark, something hit the front storm door. It wasn't the wet, scraping *shuck-shuck* of shelf-fungus dragging along the aluminum siding, and it wasn't the rhythmic *clack* of chitinous teeth testing the foundation vents. It was a fist—wrapped in padded cloth, hitting the upper safety glass in three frantic, uneven thumps that rattled the brass knocker against its plate. *Bam-bam-bam.* Marge's hand froze on the pressure canner. Across the room, Hal straightened up slowly, his hand dropping from the firewood to the hickory handle of the roofing hatchet resting against the brick mantel. "Hello?!" a voice cracked from the porch. It was high, hoarse, and muffled by a respirator, half-swallowed by the wind howling through the carport. "Hey! I see your chimney smoke! Please—my filter's iced over, I can't draw through the cartridge! Just the porch—let me on the porch!" Marge and Hal looked at each other. Nobody had knocked on that door since the sheriff's deputy came down the gravel road in April to tell them the highway south of La Pine was closed forever, and they'd found the deputy's Cruiser overgrown with yellow puffballs down by the mailbox in June. Marge looked down at the kitchen floor. There was a galvanized bucket of salted chitin-rinds sitting right beside the refrigerator waiting to go into the firebox, and three links of dark violet sausage hanging from an S-hook over the sink to dry. "Get the tub into the mudroom," Marge whispered, moving faster than a woman her size had any business moving. "Padlock the latch." Hal grabbed the bucket handle, shoved the sausages into a breadbox, and ducked into the laundry room while Marge untied her grease-spotted apron and threw it behind the flour bin. *Bam-bam!* The storm door rattled harder, a gloved palm smearing frost across the six-mil plastic taped over the inside of the glass. "Please! There's a big one down by the cattle guard, I heard it clicking!" Hal came back out of the mudroom, snapping the heavy Master Lock shut on the hasp and dropping the key into his flannel pocket. He picked up the closet-rod spear from beside the china cabinet and nodded once to Marge. Marge walked to the front door, peeled back two inches of silver foil tape from the corner of the plastic sheet to squint through the peephole, and let out a long breath through her nose. "Put the stick down, Harold," she said, reaching for the deadbolt. "It's just the mailman."

[Analysis] Chapter 5 is a strong piece of cozy-horror writing that largely delivers on its plan and the broader story's intentions. Let me examine it carefully across the relevant dimensions. STRENGTHS: The chapter opens with a beautifully grounded domestic scene. The slightly uncanny elements are handled with admirable restraint. Marge's dream about being underground trading "slow, polite chemical clicks with every spruce root between here and Klamath Falls" is the chapter's best moment—genuinely unsettling, delivered in a matter-of-fact parenthetical, and then immediately closed off with Marge's characteristic iron-bolt compartmentalization ("It was a very restful sort of dream"). The contrast between the warm, productive interior and the sudden human knocking is effective. The scramble to hide the chitin-rinds and sausages before opening the door is a nice beat that shows rather than tells the couple's awareness of how they appear to outsiders. The final line—"Put the stick down, Harold. It's just the mailman."—is a genuinely good closing beat. It's dry, it's funny, it earns its lightness, and it sets up Chapter 6 efficiently. WEAKNESSES: The chapter is somewhat thin on emotional depth. The "slicker'n snot on a brass doorknob" simile is vivid but also slightly self-conscious, the kind of folksy color that can tip into performance. The chapter follows its plan faithfully but perhaps too faithfully—it hits every beat (canning, trap description, domestic warmth, the knock at the door) in a fairly predictable sequence. There's little that surprises within the chapter itself; it functions more as a well-executed transition chapter than a chapter with its own internal arc or revelation. The plan promised "a frantic, human banging sounds at the front storm door" and delivers exactly that, no more. The metaphor "dirty sheep huddled against the fence posts" for the frozen drift-mold is good. "Slicker'n snot on a brass doorknob" is vivid if slightly try-hard. The "pump organ" simile for Hal's humming is apt. None of the metaphors are forced or purple, but none are particularly surprising either. The chapter is coherent, well-paced, and consistent with the characters as profiled. It does exactly what it needs to do as a chapter in a longer work. Its weakness is that it's more competent than inspired—it executes the plan without transcending it. "Sit," Marge ordered, pointing a thick finger at the flipped-over pickle bucket three feet from the Blaze King. "Don't touch the stove iron, you'll leave your skin on it. Put your feet on the bricks." The kid—Toby, he'd gasped out while Hal was prying the iced-over military surplus gas mask off his purple face—dropped onto the bucket like a marionette with its strings cut. He was six feet tall and didn't weigh enough to sink a canoe. Beneath three layers of raveled thrift-store sweaters, his collarbones stuck out like coat hangers, and the tips of both ears were crusted with the waxy yellow scabs of old frost-nip. Every ten seconds, his left hand twitched up to check a dead black Casio watch strapped to a wrist no thicker than a broom handle. "Lord have mercy, Toby," Hal murmured, draping a warmed moving blanket around the boy's shaking shoulders.
